
#### Step 4: aquifer, soil and distance together

```{r}
# Aquifer x permeability group, split into near and far locations; blank when fewer than 10 locations
detect_by(pathway_data, distance_group, aquifer_short, perm_group) |>
  mutate(pct_shown = if_else(n_locations >= 10, pct_detected, NA_real_)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = perm_group, y = aquifer_short, fill = pct_shown)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = if_else(n_locations >= 10, paste0(pct_detected, "%\nn=", n_locations), "")), size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ distance_group) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "% detected", direction = -1, na.value = "grey92") +
  labs(title = "Detection Rate by Aquifer, Soil Permeability and Distance",
       x = "Permeability group", y = "Aquifer type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))
```

```{r}
# Combinations with the highest detection rate (only cells with at least 15 locations)
detect_by(pathway_data, distance_group, aquifer_short, perm_group) |>
  filter(n_locations >= 15) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_detected)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

#### Putting it on the map

```{r}
# Water locations by detection status over the aquifer layer, with known PFAS sites as black triangles
water_locations_proj |>
  left_join(pathway_data |> select(hex_id, detected), by = "hex_id") |>
  filter(!is.na(detected)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = aquifer, fill = "grey95", color = "grey80") +
  geom_sf(aes(color = detected), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = pfas_sites_proj, shape = 17, color = "black", size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#eb6834", "FALSE" = "#2a78d6"),
                     labels = c("TRUE" = "PFAS detected", "FALSE" = "Not detected"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Public-water locations, detection status and known PFAS sites") +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### Does permeability change how much distance matters?

```{r}
# Logistic regression of detection on log distance and log permeability, with and without their interaction
interaction_data <- pathway_data |>
  mutate(detected_yes = as.integer(detected),
         log_distance = log1p(distance_to_nearest_site_m),
         log_ksat     = log10(ksat_100cm))

m_main <- glm(detected_yes ~ log_distance + log_ksat, data = interaction_data, family = binomial)
m_int  <- glm(detected_yes ~ log_distance * log_ksat, data = interaction_data, family = binomial)

# Likelihood-ratio test: a small p-value means the distance effect differs by permeability
anova(m_main, m_int, test = "Chisq")
tidy(m_int, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

Read the steps in order. If the detection rate falls with distance in Step 1, the source-to-receptor link is visible. If that fall is steeper in some aquifer types (Step 2) or in permeable soils (Step 3), those layers modify the distance effect, and Step 4 shows which combinations carry the highest rates. The interaction test then checks whether permeability changes the distance slope. Locations in the same system are not independent, so treat these p-values as a guide, and rely on the system-level models for the formal comparison.

### What the exploration hands to the models

The location-level work above decides what goes into the system-level models:

- **Distance** applies only to the known PFAS sites; it is the source-to-receptor link tested in Step 1 and enters every model as `log(1 + distance)`.
- **Aquifer type** was compared with risk on its own (no distance) and then against the distance link (Step 2); it enters as a whole categorical variable.
- **Soil type** (permeability, drainage, hydrologic group) was compared with risk on its own (no distance); permeability was then tested with distance (Step 3 and the interaction test). All of these soil variables enter the models at the system's highest-Hazard-Index location, and the selection decides which ones stay.
- **Missing soil or aquifer values** (join audit and the missingness tables) decide which systems are dropped, so every candidate model is fit on the same rows.

Next the locations are rolled up to one row per water system, because the public-health question is about systems.

## Water-System Level Analysis

The project's real question is how badly **public water systems** This section rolls `location_level` up to
one row per `system_name`, using `max_hazard` (the system's worst sampling point) as
the headline number, since a public-health read should not let a few clean samples
average away a real hotspot.

### Rolling locations up to systems

```{r}
# One row per system_name: worst reading, typical reading, spread, and closest known-site distance
system_hazard <- location_level |>
  group_by(system_name, system_type) |>
  summarise(
    n_hex_ids               = n(),
    max_hazard              = round(max(Hazard_Index, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    mean_hazard             = round(mean(Hazard_Index, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    hazard_range            = round(max_hazard - min(Hazard_Index, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    min_distance_to_site_m  = round(min(distance_to_nearest_site_m, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(max_hazard))

nrow(system_hazard)   # should equal n_water_systems, not n_hex_ids
system_hazard
```

```{r}
# Top 15 worst-affected systems by their single highest Hazard Index reading
top_systems <- system_hazard |> slice_head(n = 15)

ggplot(top_systems, aes(x = reorder(system_name, max_hazard), y = max_hazard)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#eb6834") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Water Systems with the Highest Hazard Index",
    x = NULL, y = "Max Hazard Index (worst sampling location)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# n_systems_above_alert = systems with at least one reading at/above the EPA limit
# (Hazard_Index = 1 means combined exposure across the four PFAS chemicals equals
# their EPA health-based reference level; above 1 means it exceeds that limit)
HAZARD_ALERT_THRESHOLD <- 1

system_hazard |>
  summarise(
    n_water_systems       = n(),
    n_systems_above_alert = sum(max_hazard > HAZARD_ALERT_THRESHOLD),
    pct_above_alert       = round(100 * mean(max_hazard > HAZARD_ALERT_THRESHOLD), 1)
  )
```

### Does spread between a system's own locations relate to its Hazard Index variability?

```{r}
# Only systems with more than one sampling location have a "spread" to measure
multi_location_systems <- location_level |>
  group_by(system_name) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  summarise(
    n_hex_ids    = n(),
    hazard_range = round(max(Hazard_Index) - min(Hazard_Index), 2),
    hazard_sd    = round(sd(Hazard_Index), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

nrow(multi_location_systems)   # how many systems this check even applies to
```

```{r}
# max_spread_m = farthest distance between any two of a system's own sampling points
system_spread <- water_locations_proj |>
  left_join(public_water1 |> distinct(hex_id, system_name), by = "hex_id") |>
  semi_join(multi_location_systems, by = "system_name") |>
  group_by(system_name) |>
  group_modify(~ tibble(max_spread_m = as.numeric(max(st_distance(.x))))) |>
  ungroup()

multi_location_systems |>
  left_join(system_spread, by = "system_name") |>
  arrange(desc(hazard_range))
```

### Do systems with spread-out locations sit on different ground types?

The check above showed that some systems have sampling locations several kilometres apart. Ground type belongs to each exact location, so the farther apart a system's locations are, the more likely they sit on different aquifer types or soil permeability classes.

```{r}
# Multi-location systems with their spread, hazard range and how many aquifer types / permeability classes they touch
span_check <- multi_location_systems |>
  left_join(system_spread, by = "system_name") |>
  inner_join(system_ground_span |> select(system_name, n_aquifer_types, n_perm_classes), by = "system_name") |>
  mutate(
    straddles_aquifers = n_aquifer_types > 1,
    straddles_perm     = n_perm_classes > 1
  )

# Systems that straddle aquifer types vs. those that do not
span_check |>
  group_by(straddles_aquifers) |>
  summarise(
    n_systems            = n(),
    median_spread_km     = round(median(max_spread_m) / 1000, 1),
    median_hazard_range  = round(median(hazard_range), 2),
    mean_hazard_range    = round(mean(hazard_range), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Same split for permeability class
span_check |>
  group_by(straddles_perm) |>
  summarise(
    n_systems            = n(),
    median_spread_km     = round(median(max_spread_m) / 1000, 1),
    median_hazard_range  = round(median(hazard_range), 2),
    mean_hazard_range    = round(mean(hazard_range), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
# Rank correlations: spread vs. number of ground types touched, and number of aquifer types vs. hazard range
span_check |>
  summarise(
    n_systems                    = n(),
    spearman_spread_aquifers     = round(cor(max_spread_m, n_aquifer_types, method = "spearman"), 3),
    spearman_spread_perm         = round(cor(max_spread_m, n_perm_classes,  method = "spearman"), 3),
    spearman_aquifers_hazardrange = round(cor(n_aquifer_types, hazard_range, method = "spearman"), 3)
  )
```

A clear positive link between spread and the number of ground types touched means the system-level ground type is a blurrier measure for wide systems. A positive link between touching more aquifer types and a larger hazard range would support the idea that the ground under a system's locations helps explain why its readings differ, and is another reason the system uses its worst location (`max_hazard`) as the outcome.

## Data Preparation for Modeling

### Outcome variable: log(max Hazard Index)

```{r}
# log1p handles Hazard_Index == 0 safely (log(0) is undefined, log1p(0) = 0)
model_data <- system_hazard |>
  filter(!is.na(min_distance_to_site_m)) |>
  mutate(log_hazard = log1p(max_hazard))
```

```{r}
# Compare raw vs. log-transformed distributions to check the log fixed the right-skew
model_data |>
  summarise(
    mean_hazard        = round(mean(max_hazard), 2),
    median_hazard      = round(median(max_hazard), 2),
    mean_log_hazard    = round(mean(log_hazard), 2),
    median_log_hazard  = round(median(log_hazard), 2)
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(model_data, aes(x = log_hazard)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#2a78d6", bins = 30) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of log(1 + Max Hazard Index) by Water System",
    x = "log(1 + Max Hazard Index)", y = "Number of water systems"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Explanatory variable: log(1 + distance to nearest site)

```{r}
# x = log(1 + raw distance): no cap applied, the full distance range is used as-is
model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(log_distance = log1p(min_distance_to_site_m))
```

```{r}
# Compare raw distance vs. its log to see how much the log compresses the range
model_data |>
  summarise(
    min_dist_m   = round(min(min_distance_to_site_m), 0),
    max_dist_m   = round(max(min_distance_to_site_m), 0),
    min_log_dist = round(min(log_distance), 2),
    max_log_dist = round(max(log_distance), 2)
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(model_data, aes(x = min_distance_to_site_m, y = log_distance)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1baf7a", alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Distance to Nearest PFAS Site vs. log(1 + Distance)",
    x = "Distance to nearest site (m)", y = "log(1 + Distance)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Simple linear regression: log(Hazard Index) on log(distance)

This is the **baseline model**: one regression line fit to every water system, with distance as the only predictor. The Tweedie and hurdle models further down are compared against it.

```{r}
# Recipe: log both the raw distance and the outcome (log-log model), no distance cap
pfas_recipe <- recipe(max_hazard ~ min_distance_to_site_m, data = model_data) |>
  step_log(min_distance_to_site_m, offset = 1) |>
  step_log(max_hazard, offset = 1)
```

```{r}
# Model spec: ordinary least squares via the "lm" engine, one predictor = "simple" regression
lm_spec <- linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm")
```

```{r}
# Workflow bundles the recipe (preprocessing) and the model spec together
pfas_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(pfas_recipe) |>
  add_model(lm_spec)

pfas_fit <- fit(pfas_workflow, data = model_data)
```

```{r}
# per 1% change in (1 + distance)
tidy(pfas_fit)
```

The log_hazard when log_distance = 0 is 0.369.
So exponential of (0.369) - 1 is about 0.45 thus the baseline prediction for a system at distance zero is a Hazard Index around 0.45 even at zero distance, which means distance alone isn't enough to push the typical prediction over the line.

The log distance estimate shows that being further away from a known site is connected to having a lower Hazard Index. There is 0.035% change in (1 + Hazard Index) per 1% increase in (1 + distance)

All these are significat to the model according to the p-values

```{r}
# glance() = one-row model fit summary (R-squared, adjusted R-squared, AIC, BIC, etc.)
glance(pfas_fit)
```

The model only explains about 1.8% which then means that distance alone cannot be used as a measure of the influence of hazard index however this r squared value is significant according to the p-value which is significantly very low

```{r}
ggplot(model_data, aes(x = log_distance, y = log_hazard)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#eb6834", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "log(Max Hazard Index) vs. log(1 + Distance to Nearest PFAS Site)",
    x = "log(1 + Distance to nearest site)", y = "log(1 + Max Hazard Index)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Candidate Predictors and Automatic Selection (AIC/BIC)

The Tweedie and hurdle models below use the same system-level table and the same automatic selection routine, so both are set up once here.

**Procedure**

1. Roll sampling locations up to one row per water system with every candidate predictor.
2. Keep systems with an aquifer match and add the transformed versions the models use.
3. Define one backward-elimination routine that works for any model and scores it by AIC or BIC.

**Key points**

- Every model starts from the same candidate variables (distance, nearby sites, aquifer, system type and all the soil variables), so results can be compared fairly.
- `n_hex_ids` is a control and is never dropped.
- `log_ksat` is soil permeability on a log10 scale at the system's highest-Hazard-Index sampling location; for logistic and Tweedie parts an effect is per 10-fold increase in permeability.
- Categorical variables (`aquifer_label`, `system_group`, `drainage_class`, `hydro_group`, `droughty_flag`) are kept or dropped as a whole, not category by category.
- The AIC/BIC choice is automatic: BIC is used when there are fewer than 20 detected systems per candidate variable, otherwise AIC (see `SELECTION_MODE` below).

### Candidate predictors at the system level

```{r}
# DISTANCE_BASIS decides which location supplies a system's distance to the known PFAS sites (pfas_sites1) and its
# count of sites within 5 km: "highest_hi_location" (the same spot as the aquifer and soil) or "nearest_any_location" (closest of its locations)
DISTANCE_BASIS <- "highest_hi_location"

# The system's representative sampling location = the one with the highest Hazard Index (ties: closest to a known PFAS site).
# Its own aquifer type and soil permeability become the system's ground type, matching how max_hazard is picked
index_location <- location_level |>
  group_by(system_name) |>
  arrange(desc(Hazard_Index), distance_to_nearest_site_m, hex_id, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(
    system_name,
    index_hex_id  = hex_id,
    aquifer_label = aquifer_label,
    log_ksat      = log10(ksat_100cm),   # soil permeability at that location, log10 scale
    index_distance_to_site_m = distance_to_nearest_site_m,
    index_sites_within_5km   = n_sites_within_5km,
    drclassdcd, hydgrpdcd, wtdepannmin, brockdepmin, slopegradwta, soc0_150, aws0_150, droughty   # the soil columns at that same location
  )

# One row per system with every candidate predictor
system_features <- location_level |>
  group_by(system_name, system_short) |>
  summarise(
    n_hex_ids              = n(),
    max_hazard             = max(Hazard_Index, na.rm = TRUE),  # unrounded so tiny readings still count as detected
    min_distance_to_site_m = min(distance_to_nearest_site_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_sites_within_5km   = max(n_sites_within_5km, na.rm = TRUE),
    nearest_any_distance_m = min_distance_to_site_m,   # kept for the comparison below
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(index_location, by = "system_name") |>
  mutate(
    min_distance_to_site_m = if (DISTANCE_BASIS == "highest_hi_location") index_distance_to_site_m else min_distance_to_site_m,
    max_sites_within_5km   = if (DISTANCE_BASIS == "highest_hi_location") index_sites_within_5km   else max_sites_within_5km
  )
```

A system with several sampling locations is represented by the location with its highest Hazard Index, the same location that sets `max_hazard`. That location's own aquifer type, soil permeability, distance to the nearest known PFAS site (from `pfas_sites1`) and count of sites within 5 km are used for the system, so the outcome, the source link and the ground type all describe the same spot. Set `DISTANCE_BASIS <- "nearest_any_location"` to take distance and site count from the closest of the system's locations instead. The two checks below show how often this choice matters.

```{r}
# Which location represents each multi-location system? tied_at_zero systems have no detection, so the tie is broken by closeness to a known site
location_level |>
  group_by(system_name) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  summarise(peak_hazard = max(Hazard_Index, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_at_peak   = sum(Hazard_Index == peak_hazard, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  summarise(
    n_multi_location_systems = n(),
    n_tied_at_zero           = sum(peak_hazard == 0),
    n_positive_peak          = sum(peak_hazard > 0),
    n_positive_peak_tied     = sum(peak_hazard > 0 & n_at_peak > 1)
  )
```

```{r}
# For multi-location systems with a positive peak: does the highest-HI location sit on a different aquifer type or permeability class than the system's other locations?
location_level |>
  group_by(system_name) |>
  filter(n() > 1, max(Hazard_Index, na.rm = TRUE) > 0) |>
  summarise(
    n_aquifers_other_locations = n_distinct(aquifer_label[Hazard_Index < max(Hazard_Index, na.rm = TRUE)], na.rm = TRUE),
    peak_aquifer               = first(aquifer_label[which.max(Hazard_Index)]),
    other_aquifers_differ      = any(aquifer_label[Hazard_Index < max(Hazard_Index, na.rm = TRUE)] != peak_aquifer, na.rm = TRUE),
    peak_perm                  = first(perm_class[which.max(Hazard_Index)]),
    other_perm_differ          = any(perm_class[Hazard_Index < max(Hazard_Index, na.rm = TRUE)] != peak_perm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n_systems                  = n(),
    n_other_locations_differ_aquifer = sum(other_aquifers_differ),
    n_other_locations_differ_perm    = sum(other_perm_differ)
  )
```

```{r}
# Does the distance basis matter? For multi-location systems, compare the highest-HI location's distance with the closest location's
system_features |>
  filter(n_hex_ids > 1) |>
  summarise(
    n_multi_location_systems = n(),
    n_distance_differs       = sum(abs(index_distance_to_site_m - nearest_any_distance_m) > 1),
    median_difference_km     = round(median(abs(index_distance_to_site_m - nearest_any_distance_m)) / 1000, 2),
    max_difference_km        = round(max(abs(index_distance_to_site_m - nearest_any_distance_m)) / 1000, 1)
  )
```

```{r}
# How much permeability varies inside one system: shows why it matters which location represents the system
location_level |>
  filter(!is.na(ksat_100cm)) |>
  group_by(system_name) |>
  filter(n() > 1) |>
  summarise(ksat_range_log10 = diff(range(log10(ksat_100cm))), .groups = "drop") |>
  summarise(
    n_multi_location_systems = n(),
    median_range_log10       = round(median(ksat_range_log10), 2),
    max_range_log10          = round(max(ksat_range_log10), 2),
    n_systems_over_10fold    = sum(ksat_range_log10 > 1)
  )
```

```{r}
# Row accounting: systems lost to a missing aquifer and/or missing permeability before the models
system_features |>
  summarise(
    n_systems             = n(),
    n_no_aquifer          = sum(is.na(aquifer_label)),
    n_no_permeability     = sum(is.na(log_ksat)),
    n_complete_for_models = sum(!is.na(aquifer_label) & !is.na(log_ksat))
  )
```

```{r}
# detected = hurdle outcome ("yes" is the SECOND level so coefficients describe the odds of detection)
# Numeric soil: missing filled with the median, then standardised so a coefficient is per 1 standard deviation
fill_z <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(if_else(is.na(x), median(x, na.rm = TRUE), x)))

hurdle_data <- system_features |>
  filter(!is.na(aquifer_label), !is.na(log_ksat)) |>
  mutate(
    detected   = factor(if_else(max_hazard > 0, "yes", "no"), levels = c("no", "yes")),
    log_hazard = log1p(max_hazard),
    # categorical soil: missing becomes "Unknown", classes under 5% of systems are lumped into OTHER
    drainage_class      = fct_lump_prop(factor(coalesce(as.character(drclassdcd), "Unknown")), prop = 0.05, other_level = "OTHER"),
    hydro_group         = fct_lump_prop(factor(coalesce(as.character(hydgrpdcd),  "Unknown")), prop = 0.05, other_level = "OTHER"),
    droughty_flag       = fct_lump_prop(factor(coalesce(as.character(droughty),   "Unknown")), prop = 0.05, other_level = "OTHER"),
    # a missing water table or bedrock depth usually means none was recorded, so it gets its own 0/1 indicator
    water_table_missing = as.integer(is.na(wtdepannmin)),
    bedrock_missing     = as.integer(is.na(brockdepmin)),
    water_table_depth   = fill_z(wtdepannmin),
    bedrock_depth       = fill_z(brockdepmin),
    slope               = fill_z(slopegradwta),
    organic_carbon      = fill_z(soc0_150),
    water_storage       = fill_z(aws0_150)
  )

# n_water_systems = rows kept; n_detected = systems that cleared the hurdle
hurdle_data |>
  summarise(
    n_water_systems = n(),
    n_detected      = sum(detected == "yes"),
    pct_detected    = round(100 * mean(detected == "yes"), 1)
  )
```

```{r}
# Audit of the prepared soil terms on the model rows: how many systems were filled in, and how many classes each categorical has
hurdle_data |>
  summarise(
    n_systems                 = n(),
    pct_water_table_missing   = round(100 * mean(water_table_missing), 1),
    pct_bedrock_missing       = round(100 * mean(bedrock_missing), 1),
    pct_slope_missing         = round(100 * mean(is.na(slopegradwta)), 1),
    pct_organic_carbon_missing = round(100 * mean(is.na(soc0_150)), 1),
    pct_water_storage_missing = round(100 * mean(is.na(aws0_150)), 1),
    n_drainage_classes        = n_distinct(drainage_class),
    n_hydro_groups            = n_distinct(hydro_group),
    n_droughty_classes        = n_distinct(droughty_flag)
  )
```

The candidate predictors are:

- **log(1 + distance to the nearest site):** the original question; distance from the system's highest-Hazard-Index location to the closest site in `pfas_sites1`. The baseline model above still uses the closest of a system's locations.
- **max_sites_within_5km:** how many known sites are nearby, not just the closest one. It overlaps with distance, so watch for unstable standard errors if both look odd.
- **n_hex_ids:** the number of sampling locations in the system (explained below).
- **aquifer_label:** the aquifer type under the system's highest-Hazard-Index sampling location.
- **log_ksat:** soil permeability (log10 ksat, top 100 cm) at the system's highest-Hazard-Index location; one unit means soil 10 times more permeable.
- **drainage_class, hydro_group, droughty_flag:** soil drainage class, hydrologic group and droughty flag at that location (missing becomes "Unknown", classes under 5% of systems are lumped into OTHER).
- **water_table_depth, bedrock_depth:** minimum annual water table depth and depth to bedrock, each with a `_missing` indicator because a missing value usually means none was recorded.
- **slope, organic_carbon, water_storage:** slope, organic carbon to 150 cm and available water storage to 150 cm.
- The numeric soil terms are filled with the median where missing and standardised, so their coefficients are per one standard deviation, not per original unit.
- **system_short:** the system type, with rare types lumped into "other".

Systems with no aquifer match (shoreline locations) or no soil permeability (open water, urban land) are dropped here, so these models use fewer systems than the baseline. A system's aquifer and permeability come from its highest-Hazard-Index sampling location, so a system whose peak location has no aquifer or soil value is dropped even if another of its locations has one. All candidate models must use the same rows for AIC/BIC to be valid, which is why the filter is applied once, here. Every soil variable is offered to the selection, which drops the ones that do not help. Systems are still required to have an aquifer and a permeability value; the other soil columns are filled in rather than dropping systems, so every model keeps the same rows.

### Why n_hex_ids is in the models

`n_hex_ids` is a **control variable**, not something we think causes contamination. `max_hazard` is the worst reading across a system's sampling locations, and systems range from 1 to 9 locations. Even if every location carried the same underlying risk, a system with 9 locations has 9 chances to catch a high reading, so its max tends to be higher, and it has more chances to detect something at all. Including `n_hex_ids` lets the other coefficients (distance, aquifer, system type) be estimated holding the number of sampling locations fixed.

Its own coefficient should not be read as "more sampling causes more PFAS." It only shows the sampling-chances effect is real. It can also overlap with system type, since large municipal systems tend to have more locations.

### Selection data and the AIC/BIC routine

```{r}
# Modeling table for the extended models: log distance, 0/1 detection flag, rare system types lumped into OTHER
selection_data <- hurdle_data |>
  mutate(
    detected_yes = as.integer(max_hazard > 0),
    log_distance = log1p(min_distance_to_site_m),
    system_group = fct_lump_prop(system_short, prop = 0.05, other_level = "OTHER")
  )

# Severity uses detected systems only
severity_selection_data <- selection_data |> filter(max_hazard > 0)
```

```{r}
# SELECTION_MODE: "auto" picks the criterion from the data (see below); set "BIC" or "AIC" to force one
SELECTION_MODE <- "auto"
sel_criteria   <- c(AIC = "AIC", BIC = "BIC")

# Every soil variable offered to the selection (prepared in hurdle_data)
soil_terms <- c("log_ksat", "drainage_class", "hydro_group", "droughty_flag",
                "water_table_depth", "water_table_missing", "bedrock_depth", "bedrock_missing",
                "slope", "organic_carbon", "water_storage")

# All candidate variables; n_hex_ids is always kept as a control
candidate_terms <- c("log_distance", "max_sites_within_5km", "n_hex_ids", "aquifer_label", "system_group", soil_terms)

# The same candidates in the hurdle recipes (raw distance and system type are transformed inside the recipe)
hurdle_terms <- c("min_distance_to_site_m", "max_sites_within_5km", "n_hex_ids", "aquifer_label", "system_short", soil_terms)

# Automatic choice: with fewer than 20 detected systems per candidate variable there are too few events for AIC to be safe, so BIC is used
n_detected_systems   <- sum(selection_data$detected_yes)
events_per_candidate <- n_detected_systems / length(candidate_terms)
SELECTION_CRITERION  <- case_when(
  SELECTION_MODE != "auto"    ~ SELECTION_MODE,
  events_per_candidate < 20   ~ "BIC",
  TRUE                        ~ "AIC"
)

tibble(n_candidate_terms = length(candidate_terms), n_detected_systems, events_per_candidate = round(events_per_candidate, 1),
       selection_mode = SELECTION_MODE, criterion_used = SELECTION_CRITERION)
```

```{r}
# Builds a formula from a vector of term names (response = NULL gives a one-sided formula)
make_formula <- function(response, terms) {
  reformulate(if (length(terms) == 0) "1" else terms, response = response)
}

# Backward elimination: drop the one term that lowers AIC/BIC the most, repeat until no drop helps
backward_select <- function(fit_fun, terms, keep = character(), criterion = c("AIC", "BIC")) {
  criterion <- match.arg(criterion)

  # Score one candidate set of terms; a failed or non-converged fit counts as infinitely bad
  score <- function(tt) {
    fit <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(fit_fun(tt)), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(fit)) return(Inf)
    if (inherits(fit, "glmmTMB") && !isTRUE(fit$sdr$pdHess)) return(Inf)
    s <- if (criterion == "AIC") AIC(fit) else BIC(fit)
    if (is.na(s)) Inf else s
  }

  current       <- terms
  current_score <- score(current)
  path <- tibble(step = 0L, dropped = "(full model)", criterion_value = current_score)

  repeat {
    droppable <- setdiff(current, keep)
    if (length(droppable) == 0) break
    trial <- map_dbl(droppable, \(d) score(setdiff(current, d)))
    if (min(trial) >= current_score) break
    worst         <- droppable[which.min(trial)]
    current       <- setdiff(current, worst)
    current_score <- min(trial)
    path <- bind_rows(path, tibble(step = nrow(path), dropped = worst, criterion_value = current_score))
  }

  list(terms = current, fit = fit_fun(current), path = path, criterion = criterion, converged = is.finite(current_score))
}

# Runs the elimination under both criteria so AIC and BIC can be compared side by side
select_both <- function(fit_fun) {
  map(sel_criteria, \(crit) backward_select(fit_fun, candidate_terms, keep = "n_hex_ids", criterion = crit))
}

# One-row-per-criterion summary of which variables survived
selection_summary <- function(sel) {
  imap_dfr(sel, \(s, crit) tibble(
    criterion       = crit,
    terms_kept      = paste(s$terms, collapse = ", "),
    n_terms_kept    = length(s$terms),
    criterion_value = round(tail(s$path$criterion_value, 1), 1),
    converged       = s$converged
  ))
}
```

```{r}
# System level: how much does the ground explain without distance? Detection model with distance only, ground only, and both
detect_sets <- list(
  "Distance only"             = c("log_distance"),
  "Ground only (no distance)" = c("aquifer_label", soil_terms),
  "Distance + ground"         = c("log_distance", "aquifer_label", soil_terms)
)

# Same rows for all three, so AIC/BIC are comparable; mcfadden_r2 near 0 means little explained
imap_dfr(detect_sets, \(tt, nm) {
  fit <- glm(make_formula("detected_yes", tt), data = selection_data, family = binomial)
  tibble(model = nm, n_systems = nobs(fit), aic = round(AIC(fit), 1), bic = round(BIC(fit), 1),
         mcfadden_r2 = round(1 - fit$deviance / fit$null.deviance, 3))
})
```

The ground-only row answers "do aquifer and soil explain detection without distance?"; the distance-only row is the source link alone; the third row shows what is gained by having both. The selection below still keeps distance as a candidate, so the ground variables are judged while holding the source link fixed.

```{r}
# Sensitivity: refit the ground-only detection model on systems whose locations all sit on ONE aquifer type
single_aquifer_names <- system_ground_span |> filter(n_aquifer_types == 1) |> pull(system_name)
ground_terms         <- c("aquifer_label", "log_ksat")   # kept small: single-aquifer systems are too few for every soil term

fit_ground_all    <- glm(make_formula("detected_yes", ground_terms), data = selection_data, family = binomial)
fit_ground_single <- glm(make_formula("detected_yes", ground_terms),
                         data = filter(selection_data, system_name %in% single_aquifer_names), family = binomial)

# n_systems used by each fit, then odds ratios side by side; similar values mean straddling systems are not driving the result
tibble(fit = c("All systems", "Single-aquifer systems only"),
       n_systems = c(nobs(fit_ground_all), nobs(fit_ground_single)))

left_join(
  tidy(fit_ground_all,    exponentiate = TRUE) |> select(term, odds_ratio_all = estimate, p_all = p.value),
  tidy(fit_ground_single, exponentiate = TRUE) |> select(term, odds_ratio_single_aquifer = estimate, p_single_aquifer = p.value),
  by = "term"
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3)))
```

A system's ground type is taken from its highest-Hazard-Index location, the same location that sets `max_hazard`. That ties the predictor to the outcome's own spot, but it also means the location was chosen by the outcome, which can overstate the link between ground type and risk. The check above, which keeps only systems that sit on a single aquifer type (where the choice of location cannot matter), is the safeguard: similar odds ratios mean the result does not depend on the choice.

**How the selection works**

- **AIC** adds a penalty of 2 per estimated parameter; **BIC** adds log(n), which is about 7 per parameter for a table of this size. BIC therefore drops weaker variables and gives the smaller model, while AIC favors predictive fit and keeps borderline variables.
- Each step removes the single variable whose removal improves the criterion the most, and stops when no removal helps. `SELECTION_CRITERION` chooses which result is used downstream. It is set automatically by `SELECTION_MODE <- "auto"`; set the mode to `"AIC"` or `"BIC"` to force one and everything below reruns on that result.
- **With about 213 detected systems and many candidate variables, the automatic rule picks BIC**, and AIC is the sensitivity check. A variable kept by both is a strong finding; a variable kept only by AIC is suggestive, not confirmed.
- The `converged` column in the selection summaries must be TRUE. FALSE means no fit in that search converged, so do not use that result (for the Tweedie, try `TWEEDIE_ZI <- FALSE`).
- Only 213 systems have a detection, so the smaller BIC model is the safer read for the severity and zero-inflation parts. After selection the p-values look somewhat better than they truly are, because the model was chosen to fit this data, and nearby systems share PFAS sites, so the rows are not fully independent. Read them as a guide, not as proof.

## Zero-Inflated Tweedie Model

About 86% of sampling locations read exactly zero and the rest are positive, right-skewed values. A **Tweedie** model is built for that shape: one model for a continuous outcome with a pile of exact zeros, fit on the raw `max_hazard`, so no `log1p` is needed. Adding **zero inflation** gives the zeros their own process, so a system can read zero because nothing was detected there (a structural zero) or because the Tweedie part happened to produce a zero.

**Procedure**

1. Fit the full zero-inflated Tweedie model on `max_hazard`, with the same candidate variables in the mean part and in the zero-inflation part.
2. Run backward elimination by AIC and by BIC; a variable is dropped from both parts together.
3. Refit the chosen variables, read both parts of the output, and compare against a plain Tweedie without zero inflation.

**Key points**

- **Mean part (log link):** the exponentiated estimate is the multiplicative change in the expected Hazard Index; for distance it should be below 1.
- **Zero-inflation part (logit link):** the exponentiated estimate is the odds of a structural zero; for distance it should be above 1, because farther systems have more zeros.
- A plain Tweedie can already produce zeros, so the zero-inflation part is weakly identified. Keep it only if AIC/BIC prefer it over the plain version.
- A fit that fails to converge is treated as infinitely bad during selection, so it can never be chosen.

```{r}
# TWEEDIE_ZI = TRUE puts the same terms in a zero-inflation part; set FALSE for a plain Tweedie if the full model will not converge
TWEEDIE_ZI <- TRUE

# Tweedie on raw max_hazard (log link); the same terms go into the mean and zero-inflation parts
fit_tweedie <- function(terms, zi = TWEEDIE_ZI) {
  glmmTMB(
    make_formula("max_hazard", terms),
    ziformula = if (zi) make_formula(NULL, terms) else ~ 0,
    family    = glmmTMB::tweedie(link = "log"),
    data      = selection_data
  )
}

# Backward elimination under both AIC and BIC, then which variables survived
tweedie_sel <- select_both(fit_tweedie)
selection_summary(tweedie_sel)
```

```{r}
# Chosen model under SELECTION_CRITERION, and the order in which variables were dropped
tweedie_pick <- tweedie_sel[[SELECTION_CRITERION]]
tweedie_pick$path
```

```{r}
# Mean part (cond) and zero-inflation part (zi); effect = exp(estimate): a ratio in cond, an odds ratio in zi
coef_table <- function(fit) {
  summary(fit)$coefficients[c("cond", "zi")] |>
    keep(\(m) !is.null(m) && nrow(m) > 0) |>
    imap_dfr(\(m, part) as_tibble(m, rownames = "term") |> mutate(part = part)) |>
    janitor::clean_names() |>
    mutate(effect = exp(estimate)) |>
    select(part, term, estimate, effect, std_error, p_value = pr_z) |>
    arrange(part, p_value)
}

coef_table(tweedie_pick$fit)
```

```{r}
# Zero-inflated vs. plain Tweedie on the same terms: power p (1 = Poisson-like, 2 = gamma-like), AIC and BIC
plain_tweedie <- fit_tweedie(tweedie_pick$terms, zi = FALSE)
tweedie_fits  <- list(tweedie_pick$fit, plain_tweedie)

tibble(
  model         = c("Zero-inflated Tweedie", "Plain Tweedie"),
  n_systems     = nrow(selection_data),
  tweedie_power = map_dbl(tweedie_fits, \(f) tryCatch(as.numeric(glmmTMB::family_params(f)), error = \(e) NA_real_)),
  aic           = map_dbl(tweedie_fits, AIC),
  bic           = map_dbl(tweedie_fits, BIC)
)
```

The lower AIC/BIC of the two rows is the preferred version. If the zero-inflated model is not clearly lower, the zero-inflation part is not adding anything and the plain Tweedie is the simpler description. If a fit prints a convergence warning, trust the selection table above, since it only accepts fits whose Hessian is well behaved.

## Hurdle Model: Detection and Severity

About 86% of sampling locations read exactly zero, so the baseline line above has to explain two different things at once: why most systems sit at zero, and how bad the contamination is in the ones that do not. That is a big reason its R-squared is so low.

A **hurdle model** splits this into two models:

1. **Part 1, detection:** a logistic regression for whether a system detects any PFAS at all (`max_hazard > 0`). It uses every system.
2. **Part 2, severity:** a linear regression of `log(1 + max_hazard)`, fit only on systems that did detect PFAS, so the zeros no longer flatten the line.

Each part can have its own significant variables, so we can see what drives detection separately from what drives severity. Poisson-type zero-inflated models are for count outcomes, so they do not fit a continuous Hazard Index; the hurdle model is the continuous-data equivalent.

### Part 1: which variables predict detection (logistic regression)

```{r}
# Log the distance, lump rare system types into "other", dummy-code the categoricals
detect_recipe <- recipe(
  make_formula("detected", hurdle_terms),
  data = hurdle_data
) |>
  step_log(min_distance_to_site_m, offset = 1) |>
  step_other(system_short, threshold = 0.05) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
```

```{r}
# Logistic regression via the "glm" engine; coefficients describe the odds of "yes" (detected)
detect_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(detect_recipe) |>
  add_model(logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm")) |>
  fit(data = hurdle_data)
```

```{r}
# exponentiate = TRUE turns estimates into odds ratios (>1 raises the odds of detecting PFAS)
tidy(detect_fit, exponentiate = TRUE) |> arrange(p.value)
```

Odds ratios above 1 mean the variable raises the odds that a system detects PFAS; below 1 lowers them. As a sanity check, the distance odds ratio should be below 1 (farther from a site means lower odds of detection); if it comes out above 1, the factor levels of `detected` are the wrong way round. For `log_ksat` the odds ratio is for soil that is 10 times more permeable; above 1 would mean more permeable soil raises the odds of detection. The standardised soil terms are per one standard deviation. Categorical variables appear as one row per category compared with a reference category, so the AIC/BIC variable selection further down (it keeps or drops each categorical as a whole) is the better way to judge whether `aquifer_label` or `system_short` matter overall.

### Part 2: which variables predict severity among detected systems (linear regression)

```{r}
# Same predictors, fit only on systems with max_hazard > 0
severity_data <- hurdle_data |> filter(max_hazard > 0)

severity_recipe <- recipe(
  make_formula("log_hazard", hurdle_terms),
  data = severity_data
) |>
  step_log(min_distance_to_site_m, offset = 1) |>
  step_other(system_short, threshold = 0.05) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
```

```{r}
severity_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(severity_recipe) |>
  add_model(linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm")) |>
  fit(data = severity_data)
```

```{r}
tidy(severity_fit) |> arrange(p.value)
```

```{r}
# One-row fit summary for the severity model
glance(severity_fit)
```

Part 2 uses far fewer rows than Part 1, because only systems with detections are included. Expect fewer significant variables here, and do not read that as "nothing matters."

## Automatic Variable Selection (Hurdle Model)

The same AIC/BIC routine defined above is applied to each hurdle part. **Hurdle** describes the two-model structure; **AIC/BIC backward selection** (and, as a cross-check, LASSO) decides which variables each part keeps.

**Procedure**

1. Fit the full plain `glm()` (detection) and `lm()` (severity) with every candidate variable.
2. Run backward elimination by AIC and by BIC and compare which variables survive.
3. Take the result for `SELECTION_CRITERION`, read its odds ratios or estimates, and refit it in tidymodels so `predict()` works.

**Key points**

- Plain `glm()`/`lm()` are used here, instead of recipes, so a categorical variable is kept or dropped as a whole rather than as separate dummy columns.
- Detection and severity can keep different variables; distance may matter for whether PFAS shows up but not for how high it gets.
- Severity uses only the detected systems, so it has far fewer rows and usually keeps fewer variables.

### Part 1: detection

```{r}
# Backward elimination for detection (logistic regression on all systems) under AIC and BIC
detect_sel <- select_both(\(tt) glm(make_formula("detected_yes", tt), data = selection_data, family = binomial))
selection_summary(detect_sel)
```

```{r}
# Chosen detection model and the order in which variables were dropped
detect_pick <- detect_sel[[SELECTION_CRITERION]]
detect_pick$path
```

```{r}
# Odds ratios for the surviving variables (>1 raises the odds of detecting PFAS), then fit summary with AIC and BIC
tidy(detect_pick$fit, exponentiate = TRUE) |> arrange(p.value)
glance(detect_pick$fit)
```

### Part 2: severity

```{r}
# Backward elimination for severity (linear regression on detected systems only) under AIC and BIC
severity_sel <- select_both(\(tt) lm(make_formula("log_hazard", tt), data = severity_selection_data))
selection_summary(severity_sel)
```

```{r}
# Chosen severity model and the order in which variables were dropped
severity_pick <- severity_sel[[SELECTION_CRITERION]]
severity_pick$path
```

```{r}
# Estimates on the log(1 + max_hazard) scale, then fit summary with R-squared, AIC and BIC
tidy(severity_pick$fit) |> arrange(p.value)
glance(severity_pick$fit)
```

### Final hurdle models refit in tidymodels (automatic)

The formulas come straight from what the selection kept, so nothing needs editing by hand when the data or `SELECTION_CRITERION` changes. The estimates match `detect_pick` and `severity_pick`; this only puts them in tidymodels form so `predict()` works.

```{r}
# Refit the detection survivors through parsnip; the formula is built from the selected terms
detect_final_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  fit(make_formula("detected", detect_pick$terms), data = selection_data)

tidy(detect_final_fit, exponentiate = TRUE) |> arrange(p.value)
```

```{r}
severity_final_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm") |>
  fit(make_formula("log_hazard", severity_pick$terms), data = severity_selection_data)

tidy(severity_final_fit) |> arrange(p.value)
```

### Cross-check: LASSO in tidymodels

LASSO adds a penalty that shrinks weak variables' coefficients to exactly zero, and whatever is left at zero is dropped. It stays inside tidymodels. Predictors are normalized so the penalty treats them fairly, so the estimates are not directly comparable to a plain `lm`/`glm`, and LASSO gives no p-values. It also drops individual dummy columns, not whole variables, and `n_hex_ids` is not protected here.

```{r}
# Same predictors as Part 1; normalize is required so the penalty treats all variables fairly
detect_recipe_lasso <- recipe(
  make_formula("detected", hurdle_terms),
  data = hurdle_data
) |>
  step_log(min_distance_to_site_m, offset = 1) |>
  step_other(system_short, threshold = 0.05) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
```

```{r}
# penalty = tune() lets cross-validation pick how aggressively to drop; mixture = 1 means LASSO
detect_lasso_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(detect_recipe_lasso) |>
  add_model(logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet"))

set.seed(123)
detect_folds <- vfold_cv(hurdle_data, v = 10, strata = detected)

detect_tuned <- tune_grid(
  detect_lasso_wf,
  resamples = detect_folds,
  grid      = grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-4, -0.5)), levels = 20),
  metrics   = metric_set(roc_auc)
)
```

```{r}
# Simplest model (largest penalty) within one standard error of the best
detect_best <- select_by_one_std_err(detect_tuned, desc(penalty), metric = "roc_auc")

detect_lasso_fit <- finalize_workflow(detect_lasso_wf, detect_best) |>
  fit(data = hurdle_data)

# Variables with a nonzero estimate survived; zeros were dropped
tidy(detect_lasso_fit) |> filter(estimate != 0)
```

```{r}
# Severity LASSO on detected systems only (severity_data defined in Part 2)
severity_recipe_lasso <- recipe(
  make_formula("log_hazard", hurdle_terms),
  data = severity_data
) |>
  step_log(min_distance_to_site_m, offset = 1) |>
  step_other(system_short, threshold = 0.05) |>
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

severity_lasso_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(severity_recipe_lasso) |>
  add_model(linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet"))

set.seed(123)
severity_folds <- vfold_cv(severity_data, v = 5)

severity_tuned <- tune_grid(
  severity_lasso_wf,
  resamples = severity_folds,
  grid      = grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-4, -0.5)), levels = 20),
  metrics   = metric_set(rmse)
)
```

```{r}
severity_best <- select_by_one_std_err(severity_tuned, desc(penalty), metric = "rmse")

severity_lasso_fit <- finalize_workflow(severity_lasso_wf, severity_best) |>
  fit(data = severity_data)

# Variables with a nonzero estimate survived; zeros were dropped
tidy(severity_lasso_fit) |> filter(estimate != 0)
```

## Model Comparison: Baseline vs. Tweedie vs. Hurdle

**Procedure**

1. Refit the baseline log-linear model on the same systems the extended models use.
2. Turn each model's output into a predicted Hazard Index on the original scale.
3. Compare prediction error and average level side by side.

**Key points**

- AIC and BIC are only comparable between models with the same outcome and the same rows, so they are used to choose variables *within* each model, not to rank the three models against each other.
- The baseline predicts `log(1 + max_hazard)`, so its predictions are converted back with `expm1()`; this tends to under-predict the average.
- The hurdle prediction is the chance of detection times the expected Hazard Index among detected systems.
- These errors are measured on the same data the models were selected on, so they are optimistic and are best read as a ranking, not as expected accuracy.

```{r}
# Baseline refit on the same systems as the extended models (log-log, distance only)
baseline_same_rows <- lm(log_hazard ~ log_distance, data = selection_data)

# Hurdle prediction = P(detected) x expected Hazard Index if detected
hurdle_p_detect <- predict(detect_pick$fit, newdata = selection_data, type = "response")
hurdle_severity <- expm1(predict(severity_pick$fit, newdata = selection_data))

comparison_data <- bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "Baseline log-linear",
         observed  = selection_data$max_hazard,
         predicted = expm1(fitted(baseline_same_rows))),
  tibble(model = "Zero-inflated Tweedie",
         observed  = selection_data$max_hazard,
         predicted = as.numeric(predict(tweedie_pick$fit, newdata = selection_data, type = "response"))),
  tibble(model = "Hurdle",
         observed  = selection_data$max_hazard,
         predicted = hurdle_p_detect * hurdle_severity)
)

# rmse and mae on the raw Hazard Index scale; mean_predicted should be close to mean_observed
comparison_data |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(
    n_systems      = n(),
    rmse           = round(sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2)), 3),
    mae            = round(mean(abs(observed - predicted)), 3),
    mean_predicted = round(mean(predicted), 3),
    mean_observed  = round(mean(observed), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Do AIC and BIC agree?

```{r}
# Variables kept by each criterion in every model; agreement between AIC and BIC marks the strongest findings
bind_rows(
  selection_summary(tweedie_sel)  |> mutate(model = "Zero-inflated Tweedie"),
  selection_summary(detect_sel)   |> mutate(model = "Hurdle: detection"),
  selection_summary(severity_sel) |> mutate(model = "Hurdle: severity")
) |>
  select(model, criterion, terms_kept, n_terms_kept) |>
  arrange(model, criterion)
```

A variable that appears under both AIC and BIC is the most reliable finding. A variable kept only by AIC (for example `log_ksat`) is supported but not confirmed, and should be reported as suggestive. If BIC keeps only `n_hex_ids` for severity, that means the few detected systems cannot support more than that, not that nothing matters; report the AIC result for severity as exploratory.

### Reading the results

- Compare the variables that survive AIC, BIC and LASSO. Variables that survive all of them are the most trustworthy.
- Detection and severity can have different important variables. For example, distance might matter for whether PFAS shows up but not for how high it gets.
- Check which soil variables survive selection and whether their direction matches the soil exploration. A soil variable that is dropped adds no information beyond the variables that stayed.
- AIC and BIC are only comparable between models with the same outcome and rows, so use them to choose variables within a model. Across the baseline, Tweedie and hurdle models, use the prediction-error table above.

## Spatial Check: Do Nearby Systems Share Leftover Error?

Nearby water systems draw from the same PFAS sites and ground, so a model can leave residuals that are clustered on the map. **Moran's I** measures that clustering in the residuals of each final model.

**Procedure**

1. Give each system one coordinate (the average of its sampling locations).
2. Link every system to its 5 nearest neighbours.
3. Test the residuals of the final Tweedie, detection and severity models for clustering.

**Key points**

- Moran's I near 0 with a large p-value means no leftover clustering, so the standard models are adequate on this point.
- A positive, significant value means neighbouring systems have similar errors; the next step would be a spatial smooth or a spatial error model.
- This chunk only runs if the `spdep` package is installed (`install.packages("spdep")`).

```{r}
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("spdep", quietly = TRUE)

# One coordinate per system: the mean of its sampling locations in the projected CRS (meters)
system_xy <- water_locations_proj |>
  left_join(public_water1 |> distinct(hex_id, system_name), by = "hex_id") |>
  mutate(x = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1], y = st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2]) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(system_name) |>
  summarise(x = mean(x), y = mean(y), .groups = "drop")

# Moran's I of a residual vector, using each system's 5 nearest neighbours
morans_i <- function(resid, data, label) {
  xy <- data |> select(system_name) |> left_join(system_xy, by = "system_name")
  lw <- spdep::nb2listw(spdep::knn2nb(spdep::knearneigh(as.matrix(xy[, c("x", "y")]), k = 5)), style = "W")
  mt <- spdep::moran.test(as.numeric(resid), lw)
  tibble(model = label, n_systems = length(resid),
         morans_i = round(unname(mt$estimate[1]), 3), p_value = signif(mt$p.value, 3))
}

bind_rows(
  morans_i(residuals(tweedie_pick$fit, type = "pearson"), selection_data,          "Zero-inflated Tweedie"),
  morans_i(residuals(detect_pick$fit,  type = "pearson"), selection_data,          "Hurdle: detection"),
  morans_i(residuals(severity_pick$fit),                  severity_selection_data, "Hurdle: severity")
)
```

## Conclusions, Limits and Next Steps

**How to read the results**

- **Baseline** shows how little distance alone explains; it is the reference point.
- **Tweedie and hurdle** show whether handling the zeros properly, and adding aquifer, soil and system type, explains more. The comparison table gives the prediction error side by side.
- **Selection tables** show which variables each model keeps under AIC and BIC; variables kept by both criteria and by LASSO are the most trustworthy.
- **Pathway section** shows where the effects come from: distance, then aquifer and soil as modifiers.

**Limits to keep in mind**

- Only about 213 systems have a detection and there are now many candidate variables (about 17 terms), so overfitting is a real risk; the automatic rule therefore uses BIC, and variables kept only by AIC are suggestive.
- Soil values are read at one location per system and numeric soil terms with missing values were filled with the median, so small soil effects should not be over-interpreted.
- Soil permeability describes the top 100 cm at the water location, while wells often draw from deeper deposits.
- Aquifer and soil are measured at the water location, not at the PFAS site.
- Systems near the same sites are not fully independent, so p-values are a guide, not proof.
- Prediction errors in the comparison table are measured on the same data used for selection, so they are optimistic.

**Next steps**

1. If the spatial check shows clustering, add a spatial smooth (a `mgcv` model) or a spatial error model.
2. If the full Tweedie model struggles to converge with this many soil variables, set `TWEEDIE_ZI <- FALSE` or screen the soil variables with the hurdle detection model first.
3. Resolve any locations with a missing system name.
4. Validate the final model on held-out systems instead of in-sample error.
